title: Cannabis Flower 101: A Beginner's Guide to Buying Bud
h1: Cannabis Flower 101: What It Is, How to Use It and How to Choose
metaDescription: A beginner guide to cannabis flower: what bud is, plant anatomy, ways to use it, premium buds vs. smalls and shake, storage and how to choose at the counter.

body:
Cannabis flower is the dried, cured bud of the cannabis plant, and it's still the product most people picture when they think of a dispensary. You can smoke it, vaporize it, roll it or cook with it, and it comes in more forms and sizes than many first-time shoppers expect. This guide covers what bud is, how to judge it at the counter and how buying it works in Michigan.

## What cannabis flower is, and why it's called bud

Cannabis flower is exactly what the name says: the flowers of the plant, harvested, dried and cured. They grow in tight, rounded clusters that resemble buds on a branch, which is where the everyday name comes from. Flower, bud and weed all describe the same thing, and dispensary menus usually say flower.

The flower that ends up in a jar comes from female plants. Growers keep male plants away so the females stay unpollinated, which means no seeds, and early research suggests more cannabinoids too. The plant's resin carries the cannabinoids and aromas people shop for.

## Where on the plant it grows

Female plants form flowers at the nodes, the points where side branches meet a stem, and in a dense cluster at the top of each main stem. That top cluster, called a cola, is usually the largest. Buds lower on the plant get less light and tend to stay smaller, which is where popcorn-size buds come from.

Cannabinoids show up throughout the plant, but they're concentrated in the female flowers. Stems, roots and the big fan leaves carry far less, and the seeds carry no significant amount. That's why flower, rather than the rest of the plant, is what's sold by the gram.

## Flower anatomy: trichomes, bracts, calyxes, sugar leaves and pistils

Look closely at a well-grown bud, or use a magnifier, and you'll see several distinct parts.

- **Trichomes:** tiny resin glands that give buds their frosty look. They make and hold most of the plant's cannabinoids and terpenes, so buyers look for a generous coating.
- **Bracts:** small, leaf-like structures that wrap around the female plant's reproductive parts. They're thick with trichomes and make up much of a bud's bulk.
- **Calyxes:** strictly speaking, a thin, see-through layer at the base of each flower. In shop talk the word is often used for bracts, so you'll hear both.
- **Sugar leaves:** small leaves poking out of the bud, dusted with trichomes. Careful trimming removes most of them from top-shelf buds, and the trimmings often go into pre-rolls or extracts.
- **Pistils:** hair-like strands that catch pollen. They start white and darken to orange or brown as the plant matures, but their color says nothing reliable about potency.

## Ways to use cannabis flower

Flower is the most flexible form of cannabis. These are the most common ways to use it:

- **Joints and pre-rolls:** ground flower rolled in paper. Pre-rolls come ready to light, while rolling your own takes a few tools and a little practice.
- **Pipes and bongs:** a pinch packed into a bowl and lit. A bong passes the smoke through water before you inhale.
- **Dry-herb vaporizers:** devices that heat ground flower until it releases vapor, without burning it.
- **Cooking:** after a gentle decarb in the oven, flower goes into homemade butter, cooking oil or a tincture.

Our [guide to cannabis accessories](/blog/guide-to-cannabis-accessories/) covers the gear for each method.

Timing differs a lot between these methods. Inhaled cannabis is typically felt within minutes and peaks in 15 to 30 minutes. Eaten cannabis usually takes 30 to 90 minutes to start working and can last for hours. Whichever you choose, go slowly and let each dose settle before you decide on more.

## Common forms: premium buds, smalls, shake and trim

The same harvest can reach the shelf at several price points. Here's how flower is commonly sold.

| Form | What it is | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Premium buds | Large, intact, carefully trimmed buds, often from the top of the plant | Joints, bowls and vapes when you want the full look and aroma |
| Smalls | Whole buds that grew small, often lower on the plant; also called popcorn buds | Everyday use at a lower price per gram |
| Shake | Loose pieces that break off buds during trimming, packing and handling | Rolling and cooking |
| Trim | Sugar leaves and small leaf bits cut away during trimming | Cooking and extracts |

Smalls and shake come from the same plants as premium buds. The differences are mostly size, looks and how much handling the material has had, which is why they cost less. Our comparison of [buds, shake and popcorn nugs](/blog/cannabis-bud-vs-shake-vs-popcorn/) goes further. To learn what sets top-shelf jars apart, see our guide to [spotting premium flower](/blog/premium-cannabis-flower-guide/).

High Society's menus list flower and pre-rolls, and the sizes and forms on offer change with what's in stock. Check your store's menu for today's selection.

## How to choose flower at the counter

Picking flower gets easier with a short checklist. Start with your senses, then read the label.

- **Aroma:** fresh flower smells distinct, whether that's citrus, pine, earth or fuel. A flat, hay-like or musty smell points to poor drying or storage.
- **Look:** buds should be intact and visibly frosty, without excess stems, seeds or any sign of mold. Color varies by strain, so don't judge by shade alone.
- **Feel:** well-kept flower is slightly springy. Buds that crumble to dust are too dry, and spongy or damp ones are too wet.
- **Label:** check the THC and CBD figures, the harvest and test dates, and the net weight. A newer harvest date usually means a fresher jar.
- **Budget:** compare price per gram rather than the sticker price. Larger sizes often cost less per gram, but only help if you'll finish them while they're fresh.

Indica, sativa and hybrid labels are a loose guide at best. In one genetic study, indica- and sativa-labeled samples weren't genetically distinct, so aroma, THC level and your own experience tell you more. When in doubt, tell your budtender how new you are and what you're hoping for. Our team is happy to help you narrow it down.

## Keeping flower fresh

Flower slowly loses aroma and potency once it's on your shelf. Heat, light and air speed that up, and over time THC breaks down into a different cannabinoid, CBN. In one four-year study, samples kept at room temperature lost nearly all of their THC, while samples kept cold and dark held up far better.

For everyday storage:

- Keep flower in an airtight glass jar sized so there isn't much empty space.
- Store it somewhere cool and dark, away from windows, stoves and hot cars.
- Aim for steady humidity. An industry standard for dried flower sets a water-activity window of 0.55 to 0.65, roughly 55 to 65 percent relative humidity in a sealed jar. Above that range mold becomes a risk, and below it buds turn brittle.
- Keep it well away from children and pets.

Our [cannabis storage guide](/blog/how-to-store-marijuana/) has more detail, including edibles and concentrates.

## Buying flower in Michigan: weights, limits and ID

Flower is sold by weight, in sizes named for fractions of an ounce. Menus round an ounce to 28 grams, so the common sizes are one gram, an eighth (3.5 grams), a quarter (7 grams), a half (14 grams) and an ounce (28 grams). Our guide to [grams, eighths and ounces](/blog/how-many-grams-ounce-marijuana/) explains how far each size goes.

Michigan law sets clear limits for adults 21 and older:

- A licensed adult-use store may sell no more than 2.5 ounces in a single transaction, and no more than 15 grams of that as concentrate.
- You may carry up to 2.5 ounces, with no more than 15 grams as concentrate.
- At home, you may keep up to 10 ounces plus whatever your own plants produce, but anything over 2.5 ounces must be locked up.

Have your government-issued photo ID with you. Recreational shopping is available to individuals 21 years or older, and individuals 18 and older with a medical marijuana card can also make purchases. At High Society, you can browse your store's menu in our [online shop](/shop/) and order ahead for pickup, or shop in person with a budtender. Enjoy cannabis responsibly, and don't travel across state lines with cannabis.

faq.q: Is cannabis flower the same thing as weed?
faq.a: Yes. Flower, bud and weed all mean the dried, cured flowers of the cannabis plant. Flower is the word most dispensaries use on their menus, while weed is the casual version. Vapes, edibles and concentrates are made from the plant too, but they're processed products rather than flower itself.

faq.q: How are shake and popcorn buds different?
faq.a: Popcorn buds, also called smalls, are whole buds that simply grew small, usually lower on the plant where light is weaker. Shake is the loose material that breaks off buds during trimming, packing and handling. Smalls tend to keep more of their structure and aroma, while shake suits rolling and cooking. Both come from the same plants as bigger buds.

faq.q: How much flower should a first-time buyer get?
faq.a: Start small. A single gram or an eighth (3.5 grams) is enough to learn how a strain suits you without a big commitment. A small amount also stays fresh, because you'll finish it sooner. Once you find something you enjoy, larger sizes usually cost less per gram.

faq.q: How long will flower stay fresh?
faq.a: Stored airtight, cool and dark, flower keeps its quality for months, though the aroma fades first. Potency drops more slowly as THC breaks down into CBN, and light and warmth speed that up. In a four-year study, room-temperature samples lost nearly all of their THC, while cold, dark samples held up far better.

faq.q: When picking flower, what matters most?
faq.a: Use your senses, then the label. Look for intact, frosty buds without mold, seeds or excess stems, and a fresh, distinct smell rather than a musty one. Check the THC figure and the harvest and test dates. Then tell your budtender how experienced you are and what you're after, and they can point you to options that fit.
